newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban set up committee to tackle food crisis.
newsitem.headline: Taleban set up committee to tackle food crisis.

text.p: The purist Islamic Taleban have set up a committee and cut taxes to tackle a food crisis that driven up wheat flour prices, a senior Taleban official said on Thursday.

The committee, made up of officials from the ministries of Foreign Affairs, Finance, Interior and Commerce, aims to create and implement a plan to bring food to Afghanistan, Taleban Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said.
As part of the plan, the Taleban administration has given tax exemptions on imports of wheat flour, edible oil, tea, sugar and rice, he said.
Price of wheat flour and bread have risen recently due to supply problems. Most of Afghanistan's wheat comes from its eastern neighbour Pakistan, which is also suffering from a severe wheat shortage.
Dwindling food supplies have sparked riots in several Pakistani cities in the past week.

The shortage in Kabul has seen prices rise by 40 percent over the last few days. Terry Pitzner, the head of the United Nations refugee agency in Kabul, told Reuters on Wednesday that bread prices were beyond the reach of many of Kabul's citizens and urged the Taleban authorities to take action.
"Bread is now out of the reach of the most destitute families. I urge the Afghan authorities to take action to resolve this shortage of wheat flour." said Pitzner.
Mutaqi said the Taleban had received an encouraging response from flour traders about alleviating the problem, and said he hoped this year's harvest would be solid.
"We have talked with traders and their views were promising. We had plenty of rain this year and, God willing, when the harvest comes in we will have plenty of wheat." he said.
Mutaqi partially blamed the shortage on the previous government, whom the Taleban drove from Kabul last September.

"The government stock of wheat has been looted by the previous government. They took all the wheatstocks. We have done all we could. We have opened the roads. We have not brought this crisis." he said.
Mutaqi told journalists did not believe that the shortages would create unrest among Kabul's hard-pressed population.
"Our nation will not be upset by the rise in prices because our leaders eat the same dishes as the ordinary people, unlike the previous regime who didn't care," he said.
The head of the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) in Afghanistan, Anis Haider, expressed concern about the situation.

"We are worried that the current situation will increase the number of vulnerable people in the city and we are therefore trying to work out how best to deal with the problem," Haider said in a statement, released on Wednesday.
He said a large proportion of Kabul's residents were already receiving food aid from the WFP.
"WFP is now feeding 25-30 percent of the Kabul population -- the most vulnerable people -- through subsidised bakeries, food-for-work schemes and hospitals." he said.
